title: "이 날씨에 회 먹어도 되나요?"...이 감염균, 지병 있다면 '치명적'
content: The Korean Food and Drug Administration (식품의약품안전처) warned on September 5, 2025 that the ongoing heatwave and rising sea temperatures could trigger outbreaks of Vibrio food poisoning. Vibrio bacteria begin to multiply when seawater reaches 15°C and grow rapidly between 20°C and 37°C (장염 비브리오균은 바닷물 온도가 15도 이상이 되면 증식을 시작해 20~37도에서 매우 빠르게 증식한다). Consuming raw shellfish contaminated with Vibrio can cause vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Vibrio septicemia bacteria are most active during the warm months of May to October (비브리오 패혈증균은 수온이 상승하는 5~10월에 활발히 증식한다). People with underlying chronic liver disease are at risk of fatal septic shock if infected (만성 간질환 등 기저질환이 있는 사람이 감염되는 경우 패혈성 쇼크로 사망할 수 있다). The agency is testing aquarium water in seafood restaurants for Vibrio contamination and has launched a Vibrio Prediction System (vibrio.foodsafetykorea.go.kr/main) that provides real‑time forecasts for popular fishing spots, tide points, and beaches (비브리오 예측시스템은 ... 실시간으로 공개하고 있다고 전했다). Travelers are urged to check the system before visiting beaches to avoid infection (식약처는 '여행객이 해수욕장 등을 방문할 때는 비브리오균으로 인한 피해가 발생하지 않도록 사전에 비브리오 예측시스템을 확인해달라'고 당부했다).

title: New vaccine for typhoid, salmonella shows promise
content: A new vaccine targeting both typhoid and non-typhoid salmonella has shown promising results in a Phase 1 clinical trial conducted by researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine and published in Nature Medicine on October 8, 2025. Lead investigator Dr. Wilbur Chen stated, 'These results are highly encouraging,' highlighting the vaccine's potential to protect children in regions where both diseases are endemic and deadly. The trial involved 22 healthy adults randomized to receive either a low dose, high dose, or placebo of the vaccine. All participants developed a strong immune response to the vaccine components, even at lower doses, with only minor injection site pain reported. The vaccine is derived from sugar molecules taken from the outer coating of Salmonella typhi (which causes typhoid) and two common non-typhoid salmonella strains. It was developed in collaboration with Bharat Biotech International Limited (BBIL) in India. According to the CDC, salmonella causes about 1.35 million infections annually in the U.S., while typhoid fever remains a life-threatening illness often contracted during international travel and a major cause of child mortality in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: 올해만 8명 숨졌다...'치명률 42%' 비브리오패혈증 급증
content: Vibriosis sepsis, a bacterial infection caused by Vibrio species, has surged in South Korea in 2025. According to the Korea Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (KCDC), only 1–2 cases were reported in July 2025, but 14 cases were reported in August alone. The cumulative total for 2025 up to September 16 is 19 cases, of which 8 patients died, giving a fatality rate of 42.1 %. This represents a 9.5 % decline from the 21 cases reported in the same period of 2024, yet the fatality rate remains high. All 8 deaths occurred in patients with underlying conditions such as liver disease, malignancy, or diabetes, placing them in a high‑risk group. Vibriosis sepsis is transmitted through consumption of raw or undercooked seafood or contact of open wounds with contaminated seawater, with an incubation period of 12–72 hours. Symptoms include acute fever, chills, hypotension, vomiting, and within 24 hours skin lesions such as rash, edema, or hemorrhagic blisters; severe cases can lead to death. The infection peaks during the warm months of August to October when sea temperatures rise. Prevention measures recommended by the KCDC include storing seafood at ≤5 °C, cooking it to ≥85 °C, wearing gloves when handling seafood, and disinfecting cutting boards and knives. 임승관, head of the KCDC, said, '비브리오패혈증 예방을 위해서는 어패류, 게, 새우 등 익히지 않은 음식 섭취를 피하는 것이 중요하며, 특히 간 질환, 당뇨병 등 기저 질환을 가진 고위험군은 비브리오패혈증 예방 수칙을 각별히 숙지하고 지켜달라' .

title: Salmonella nedir? Gıda zehirlenmesine karşı aşı geliştiriliyor
content: A team of scientists from the University of Maryland is developing a vaccine against Salmonella, a major cause of foodborne illness, with promising early results. The vaccine, called TSCV (Trivalent Salmonella Conjugate Vaccine), targets three distinct Salmonella serovars: Salmonella Typhi, which causes typhoid fever, and two others known to cause severe infections in children. In Phase 1 clinical trials involving 22 healthy adult volunteers in the U.S., the vaccine was found to be safe, well-tolerated, and effective in triggering a strong immune response, with the only reported side effect being mild pain at the injection site. According to co-author Prof. Myron Levine, 'These findings establish a strong foundation for future studies.' Salmonella infections, which commonly stem from undercooked meat, poultry, eggs, or unwashed produce—and occasionally from person-to-person contact—cause over 1 million cases annually in the U.S., leading to thousands of hospitalizations. The disease poses a significant risk to young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. The study's small scale does not diminish its significance, as the results indicate substantial potential for TSCV to become a vital preventive tool, particularly in regions where children are most vulnerable.

title: Unmasking Vibrio paracholerae: Genomic Reclassification and Epidemiology
content: The study examined more than 13,000 Vibrio cholerae genomes in GenBank and applied Mash, whole‑genome average nucleotide identity (gANI), and digital DNA‑DNA hybridization (dDDH) to reclassify 193 unique genomes as Vibrio paracholerae, while no Vibrio metoecus or Vibrio tarriae were detected. Phylogenomic analysis revealed that V. paracholerae forms distinct but relatively homogeneous lineages that span clinical, environmental, and animal sources over a period exceeding a century. Virulence profiling showed the absence of CTX and TCP, yet most genomes carried hemolysins, RTX toxins, colix toxin, and a conserved type VI secretion system. Resistome analysis identified multiple antibiotic resistance genes, many embedded in superintegrons, underscoring V. paracholerae’s role as a reservoir of resistance determinants. Two genomic markers with high discriminatory power were identified, providing robust tools for species identification and epidemiological surveillance. These results emphasize the relevance of V. paracholerae for clinical and epidemiological monitoring.

title: Vaccine for typhoid, invasive Salmonella shows promise in phase 1 trial
content: An international team of researchers, led by the University of Maryland (UM) School of Medicine's Center for Vaccine Development and Global Health (CVD) and Bharat Biotech International Limited, reported promising results from a phase 1 trial of a novel trivalent Salmonella conjugate vaccine (TSVC). The vaccine targets Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid fever), and serovars Typhimurium and Enteritidis (invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella, iNTS), which together cause the majority of severe bloodstream infections in children in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). In a small trial of 22 healthy US adults aged 18 to 45, TSVC was safe and well-tolerated, with no serious adverse events and only mild to moderate solicited reactions. All participants who received the vaccine—either low dose (6.25 µg) or high dose (12.5 µg)—mounted a strong immune response to all three polysaccharide components within 28 days, and the flagellin carrier proteins elicited responses in 7 out of 8 low-dose recipients and all high-dose recipients. No immune response was observed in placebo recipients. Antibody levels remained fourfold higher than baseline more than a year after vaccination, despite delays due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Lead investigator Wilbur Chen, MD, stated the results are 'highly encouraging' and suggest TSVC has the potential to protect children in regions where both typhoid and iNTS are endemic. The vaccine may also benefit high-income countries where Salmonella Enteritidis and Typhimurium cause common foodborne illness. The researchers plan to conduct a trial in young infants and toddlers in SSA, followed by a large phase 3 field trial to assess protective efficacy, and evaluate co-administration with routine childhood vaccines. The findings were published in Nature Medicine on October 8, 2025.

title: انجاز تاريخي.. لقاح واحد يحمي من التيفوئيد والسالمونيلا
content: Researchers at the University of Maryland have reported successful results from the first clinical trials of a novel vaccine, named the 'trivalent conjugate Salmonella vaccine,' which protects against typhoid fever and invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS) infections. The vaccine uses sugar molecules derived from the outer capsule of Salmonella Typhi (the typhoid-causing bacterium) and two other non-typhoidal Salmonella strains, linked to specific proteins to enhance immune recognition and response. In a randomized trial involving 22 healthy adult volunteers in the United States, participants received low or high doses of the vaccine or a placebo. Results published in the journal 'Nature Medicine' showed the vaccine was safe and well-tolerated, with only mild and temporary side effects. All recipients developed strong immune responses against all three bacterial strains, while no response was observed in the placebo group. Lead researcher Professor Wolber Chen stated the findings are 'highly encouraging,' suggesting the vaccine could provide effective protection for children in regions where typhoid and Salmonella cause high mortality. The vaccine has potential to reduce Salmonella foodborne illnesses in the U.S., which cause approximately 1.35 million infections and over 26,000 hospitalizations annually, particularly from undercooked poultry, eggs, or contaminated vegetables. Some participants showed pre-existing antibodies, indicating prior exposure via foodborne illness, which may have enhanced their immune response. The research team is now evaluating the vaccine’s efficacy in children and infants, the most vulnerable group in sub-Saharan Africa. Co-researcher Professor Myron Levine, founder of the university’s Vaccine Development Center, emphasized that the current results provide a strong foundation for advancing to larger-scale trials involving children. The vaccine was developed in collaboration with India’s 'Bharat Biotech' using the WHO-approved 'Taypar TCV' platform. According to University of Maryland School of Medicine Dean Mark Gladwin, sub-Saharan Africa reported over 420,000 Salmonella cases and 66,000 deaths in 2017, along with 650,000 typhoid cases and 9,000 deaths, stating that a single vaccine protecting against both diseases would be a 'game-changer' for global child health.

title: Hautverletzung am Meer? Warum du jetzt ganz genau hinschauen solltest
content: Vibrio bacteria are multiplying in the North and Baltic Seas due to the high water temperatures this summer. People with pre-existing conditions should seek medical attention immediately if they experience severe pain after a skin injury while swimming in the sea. The infection can progress rapidly. Older people and those with pre-existing conditions such as diabetes or cancer should be cautious when the water temperature exceeds 20°C. While swimming is generally safe for healthy people, those with certain pre-existing conditions should avoid the water. According to the Landesamt für Gesundheit und Soziales in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (Lagus), high water temperatures promote the growth of Vibrio bacteria, which can cause severe and even deadly infections. This year, a 68-year-old man with multiple chronic conditions died from a Vibrio infection in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Lagus warns that open wounds, especially in older people or those with weakened immune systems, can lead to sepsis and death. 'If bathers belong to a high-risk group and have skin injuries, they should avoid contact with sea or brackish water,' Lagus advises. Symptoms of infection include chills, diarrhea, fever, or skin rash. Those with pre-existing conditions and skin injuries should seek medical attention immediately. Treatment involves antibiotics. People with the following pre-existing conditions are at risk: diabetes, cancer, weakened immune system, or open wounds. Additionally, all bathers should be aware of 'sea saw' (Blaualgen), which can be recognized by green or blue streaks in the water. If visibility is reduced to less than one meter, it is recommended to avoid swimming. In freshwater areas, cercariae (larvae of tapeworms) can also occur, causing itchy pustules and blisters on the skin.

title: Sinsi tehlike: Et yiyen bakteri can alıyor, vaka sayıları arttı! Küçük bir çizik neredeyse hayatına mâl olacaktı
content: The article reports a growing public‑health concern in the United States about the bacterium *Vibrio vulnificus*, known as the "meat‑eating bacterium." According to the CDC, the number of cases along the U.S. coast rose by 800 % between 1988 and 2018, with roughly 80 000 infections each year, about 30 000 of which are linked to water exposure. In 2025, Massachusetts confirmed 71 cases, 30 % of which required hospitalization, but no deaths were recorded. The piece cites a tragic incident in New Orleans where Linard Lyons suffered a small cut that became infected; he was treated in the emergency department, underwent surgery, and survived with a 50 % chance of survival reported by his doctors, while the overall mortality risk for *Vibrio* infections is about 30 % if treatment is delayed. The article also notes that nine people died in Louisiana and Florida from the bacterium. In Turkey, the Ministry of Health has not reported any confirmed cases, but experts warn that the bacterium can thrive in warm, salty waters and can be transmitted through open wounds or consumption of raw shellfish. Prof. Dr. Fatma Nurhayat Saydam emphasizes that the risk is highest from May to October, especially in areas where freshwater mixes with seawater, and advises avoiding swimming with open wounds and refraining from eating raw or under‑cooked shellfish. The article includes several direct quotes, such as ‘Vibrio vulnificus’ and ‘derinin altındaki dokuyu etkileyen’ necrotizing fasciitis, to illustrate the severity of the infection.
